A-02.question: How do I create my first analysis?
A-02.answer:

2. **Submit.** Caspr reads the prompt and asks a short round of clarifying questions — scoping details it needs to target the report precisely, such as timeframe, geography, or the audience the report is for. Answer what you can; there is no wrong answer here, this step exists to catch gaps before any research runs.

3. **Review the layout.** Caspr proposes a structured layout — the report's table of contents, section by section, before a word is written. Add, remove, or reorder sections if you want to steer the output further. This is the scope you're actually paying for.

4. **Confirm at the gate.** One screen shows exactly what will be produced — depth, output formats, language, style, and price — all pre-set by Caspr, all changeable. Your first analysis is covered by the $100 Research Budget you start with, so there's nothing to weigh here.

5. **Hit Generate.** Caspr runs. Generation is atomic — no pausing, no mid-run edits — so you can watch it build in Theater, or step away entirely. Most analyses finish in under 15 minutes.

6. **Receive your report.** A boardroom-ready PDF, up to 100 pages, every insight cited to its source, ready to open the moment it lands.

That's the entire loop, start to finish, faster than a coffee break.

A-03.question: What should I type in the prompt box?
A-03.answer:
A strong prompt names three things: the subject, the market or geography, and the decision it needs to inform. You don't need a paragraph — one precise line beats five vague ones.

Weak: "Tell me about the fintech industry."
Strong: "Competitive landscape of B2B payments fintechs in Southeast Asia, for a market-entry decision."

A few examples across use cases:

- **Investor, deal sourcing:** "Market size and growth drivers for veterinary telehealth in the US, for an early-stage investment thesis."
- **Consultant, client deliverable:** "Business case for a mid-market grocery chain entering quick-commerce in Brazil."
- **Category manager:** "Competitive landscape and pricing benchmarks for private-label snacks in UK retail."
- **Corporate development:** "Acquisition targets in European industrial IoT, sub-$200M revenue."

Notice the pattern in every one: subject, geography, decision. That's what turns a general topic into a report someone can act on, rather than a summary of a Wikipedia page.

You will not get this wrong. If your prompt is thin — just an industry name, no geography, no stated purpose — Caspr asks clarifying questions before it runs anything. It scopes the gaps: which markets count as competitors, what timeframe matters, who the report is ultimately for. That round exists precisely so a one-line prompt is enough to start; you don't need to anticipate every detail up front.

The layout proposal that follows is your second checkpoint. Before any research runs, Caspr shows you the report's structure — the sections it intends to build — and you can add, remove, or reorder before confirming. Between the prompt, the clarifying questions, and the layout, there is no version of this where you're locked into the wrong report with no way back.

B-01.question: What is Analytical AI, and how is it different from Generative AI?
B-01.answer:
Analytical AI is purpose-built to analyse: it takes a business question, reasons through data, structures a conclusion, and cites every source. Generative AI is purpose-built to converse: it predicts the next plausible word from patterns in its training data. Both use large models. They are built for opposite jobs.

Ask a generative model for a market analysis and it drafts fluent prose that sounds authoritative, assembled from probability, not evidence. It can invent a statistic, misattribute a source, or answer confidently on data it never saw. That is not a flaw to patch; it is the job it was built for — conversation, not analysis.

Caspr is Analytical AI. Type a single-line prompt, and Caspr proposes a structured layout, asks the clarifying questions an analyst would ask, then delivers a ~100-page boardroom-ready PDF or editable PPTX in under 15 minutes — every insight cited to a credible source, drawn from 1M+ curated documents, government databases, and news feeds. No scraping, no invention.

Three stages do the work. Assessment is the research methodology: it reasons through the data and structures the conclusions, rather than retrieving and paraphrasing snippets. Sourcing is the live data layer: it pulls from real-time feeds, so the analysis reflects today's market, not a training cutoff from months or years ago.

The distinction matters commercially, not just technically. A chatbot gives you a starting point you still have to verify line by line. Caspr gives you a document you can put in front of a board, because you can trace every claim back to its source before anyone in the room asks where the number came from.

That's why consultants, investors, and strategy teams reach for Caspr instead of a chat window when the deliverable is a market sizing, a competitive landscape, or a due-diligence screen. Generative AI is excellent at drafting an email or a first pass at a pitch. It was never built to defend a number in a boardroom — and it shouldn't have to be, because that was never the job.

While the world was building generative AI, we built analytical AI.

B-02.question: How does Caspr handle sources that disagree?

Most AI tools retrieve: they search a corpus, pull the closest-matching snippets, and stitch them into a paragraph. Assessment reasons: it works through the data the way a senior analyst would, weighing sources against each other and building toward a conclusion, not just returning what it found first.

In practice, this is what separates a report from a lookup. When you prompt Caspr, the assessment stage proposes a structured layout for the analysis, asks the clarifying questions that sharpen scope, then works through the relevant sources to construct each section's argument — figures, comparisons, and conclusions that follow from the evidence, not just sit beside it. Every insight it produces carries its source, so the reasoning can be checked, not just trusted.

This is why a Caspr report reads like something an analyst wrote, not something a search engine assembled. A market-sizing section doesn't just list numbers pulled from different reports — it reconciles them, flags where sources disagree, and lands on a defensible estimate. A competitive landscape doesn't just describe competitors — it structures them against the dimensions that matter to your question.

Assessment runs on every analysis, from a $15 Brief to a $300 Intelligence report. Deeper depths simply give it more scope to reason through, not a different method.

It's paired with the sourcing stage, Caspr's live data layer, so the reasoning is always applied to current information rather than a fixed, ageing dataset. One structures the argument; the other keeps the facts underneath it current. Neither replaces judgment — both are built so the reader can check the judgment for themselves, source by source.

B-03.question: How current is Caspr's data?
B-03.answer:
Sourcing is Caspr's live data layer — the system that keeps every analysis current. A trained model's knowledge is frozen at the point its training data was collected; ask it about this quarter's numbers and it either doesn't know or guesses. Sourcing pulls from real-time feeds, so the analysis reflects today's reality, not a training cutoff.

This matters most exactly when it's least convenient to ignore: a market that moved this quarter, a competitor that just raised a round, a regulation that changed last month. A model trained months ago will describe the market as it stood when that training data was collected. Caspr's sourcing checks against live sources — documents, government databases, news feeds — as the report is built, so the figures and events in your analysis are current, not stale.

Paired with the assessment stage, which structures the reasoning, the sourcing stage supplies the facts to reason with. Together they're why a Caspr report can cite a source published last week as readily as one published last year, and why its conclusions hold up when someone in the room checks them against this morning's news.

For anything time-sensitive — a live deal, a fast-moving category, a board update due this quarter — the sourcing stage is the difference between an analysis that was true and one that still is.

This is also the practical reason Caspr doesn't simply run on a fixed, pre-indexed dataset. A market can shift meaningfully in the weeks between a training run and the day you need an answer. Sourcing is built so that gap never shows up in your report.

Caspr's source base is curated the way a research desk builds its library: government statistics agencies, regulatory filings, industry databases, and vetted news, selected because they can be checked.

Sourcing keeps this source base live, pulling current data as each analysis runs, so a report built today reflects today's filings and this week's news, not a stale index built once and left to age.

Caspr avoids this by construction, not by caution. Every insight in a report is generated from a specific, cited source — one of 1M+ curated documents, government databases, and live data feeds. That's why every claim carries a red-dot citation you can click and verify yourself, and why the full source list sits on the report's last page. Zero hallucinations doesn't mean "trust us." Generative AI cannot promise that won't happen — it wasn't built to know the difference between a real number and a convincing one. The practical test: can you hand the output straight to someone whose job is to find the hole in it? A chat transcript needs verification before it earns that trust. A Caspr report is built to survive it.

This isn't a knock on ChatGPT — it's an excellent tool for what it was built to do: draft, summarise, brainstorm, converse. Research that has to hold up under scrutiny is a different job, with a different bar. Caspr was purpose-built for that bar.

See the difference.

C-01.question: What is the structured layout proposal?
C-01.answer:
After you submit your prompt and answer Caspr's clarifying questions, Caspr proposes a structured layout — the skeleton of your report, section by section, before a single page gets written.

This is the checkpoint between "Caspr understood my question" and "Caspr is about to spend my budget answering it." Rather than running the full analysis blind and hoping the structure lands, Caspr shows you the plan first: what sections it intends to build, in what order, at what depth for the Tier you've chosen. A Brief comes back as a flat list of sections. A Study or Intelligence report comes back nested — sections with sub-sections beneath them — because there's more ground to cover and more structure needed to hold it.

You review the layout the way you'd review an analyst's outline before they disappear for a week to write the memo, except here it takes seconds, not a meeting. If the layout covers what you actually need answered, you move forward. If something's missing, or a section doesn't belong, you can add, remove, or reorder it before Caspr runs a single word.

The layout is the scope. It's the last point where you shape what the report becomes without touching the analysis itself. Once you're satisfied, the next stop is the gate, where Tier, formats, language, and price get their final confirmation before generation starts. Think of it as the difference between briefing a junior analyst and reading their finished memo — Caspr lets you brief first, and see the outline before you commit.

C-02.question: Can I change the layout before it runs?
C-02.answer:
Yes. Once Caspr proposes the layout — the report's skeleton — you can reshape it before anything runs.

To add a section, use the add-section control on the layout screen and it drops into the outline wherever you place it. To remove one, select it and choose remove — Caspr won't build a section you don't need, and won't charge for it either. To reorder, drag a section to where it should sit; the sequence you land on is the sequence Caspr writes in, from the executive summary through to the closing exhibits.

This is the one moment before generation where you steer the report directly, without touching a single word of the analysis itself. Missing a competitor comparison you know the board will ask about? Add the section. Got a section proposed that doesn't matter for this particular decision? Cut it, and Caspr won't spend budget researching it. Want the market context up front instead of buried in the middle? Drag it there.

Get the layout right here, and everything Caspr builds afterward answers the question you actually asked, not the question it guessed at. Once you're satisfied with the structure, move on to the gate, where Tier, output formats, language, and price get their final confirmation before you generate.

There's no limit on how many changes you make, and no penalty for taking your time over it — Caspr hasn't spent any of your budget yet. Treat the layout the way you'd treat an outline you're about to hand to a research team: read it once for what's missing, once for what's redundant, and adjust until it matches the brief in your head, not just the brief Caspr inferred from your prompt.

C-03.question: How do I choose the right depth for my question?
C-03.answer:
Match the depth to the decision, not the topic. Caspr offers three depths, all drawing from your Research Budget at a fixed price:

- A quick fact-check or a single scoped question → Brief ($15).
- A full market or competitive analysis → Study ($80).
- A board-grade deep dive or due-diligence screen → Intelligence ($300 in-budget, $399 à la carte; unlocks at Business).

The test is what the output has to withstand. If you need one sourced answer to move forward, a Brief is enough. If you are producing the analysis itself — a market sizing, a competitor map, a business case someone will act on — a Study is the right floor. If the decision is high-stakes and the report will sit in front of a board or an investment committee, Intelligence gives you the broader sourcing and deeper reasoning to defend it.

Cost scales with depth, and so does what you can stake on the result. A $15 Brief and an $80 Study both return a cited, structured report in under 15 minutes; Intelligence goes further where the decision warrants it.

Two practical notes. You can start shallow and go deeper — run a Brief to scope the question, then commit to a Study. And Premium Data Add-ons ($20–60, opt-in and priced before the run) can strengthen any depth when a market is hard to source.

Not sure? Start with a Study — the best first look at a full Caspr report.

Pick a depth.

C-04.question: What is a Premium Data Add-on, and when is it worth it?
C-04.answer:
A Premium Data Add-on pulls from a higher tier of sourcing than Caspr's standard research — databases and datasets that cost more to license because they're harder to get, more current, or more authoritative for a specific market. It's shown to you at the gate, priced between $20 and $60, before you commit to anything.

It's opt-in, always. Caspr never adds it silently and never bills you for it without your say — you see the add-on, see the price, and decide whether the extra spend earns its keep on this particular analysis. There's no default-on toggle to catch you off guard.

When is it worth it? When the stakes or the market make standard sourcing thin. A market-sizing report on a well-covered US sector rarely needs it — Caspr's 1M+ curated sources already cover that ground well. A due diligence brief on a niche vertical, an emerging market with sparse public data, or a decision with real money riding on it is a different case: the add-on is what closes the gap between "good enough" and "defensible in the room."

The rule of thumb: if the analysis is informing a decision you'd hate to get wrong, or the subject is one where public data is genuinely scarce, the add-on is cheap insurance against citing a weaker source than the question deserves. If neither is true, skip it — Caspr's standard sourcing is built to be sufficient on its own, and you're not paying for depth you don't need.

Either way, you decide before you generate, never after. The price you see at the gate is the price you pay.

C-05.question: Can I upload my own data?
C-05.answer:
Yes — at the Business milestone. Upload your own files and Caspr folds them into the analysis alongside its 1M+ curated sources, instead of working from public data alone.

This is where proprietary numbers earn their keep: your internal sales figures, a client's data room, last quarter's board deck, a dataset no competitor has access to. Upload it, and Caspr treats it as source material — reasoned through and cited, the same way it treats any external document — so the report reflects your actual numbers blended with the market context around them, not just what's publicly available.

Data upload lives in the Data Room, alongside Intelligence-depth analyses and editing, as one of the capabilities that unlock at Business ($600/month). Below that milestone, Caspr works from its own curated sources only — still 1M+ documents, databases, and feeds, just without your own files in the mix.

If your work regularly starts from data no one else has — a due diligence data room, a proprietary tracker, internal figures a public report could never capture — this is the milestone where Caspr stops being a market researcher and starts being an analyst who's read your files too. Once uploaded, manage what Caspr actually uses from your Data Room, file by file: mark a file Included and it's attached to analyses by default, or Excluded and it's kept but never used unless you opt it in for a specific run. Nothing you upload gets folded into a report silently — you decide what's in scope every time.

C-06.question: Can I run multiple analyses at once?
C-06.answer:
Yes. Each analysis you start is its own run, drawing its own budget from your Research Budget — there's no shared queue slowing one report down because another is already in progress.

Start three analyses back to back and each still completes in its own sub-15-minute window; running more than one doesn't push any of them further out, because Caspr isn't processing them in a single line. The only real limit is your budget: each analysis costs what its Tier costs — Brief, Study, or Intelligence — deducted as it runs, and your total spend is whatever the sum of what you've started comes to.

That means you can send a Brief on one market while a Study runs on another, and check back on both inside fifteen minutes. There's no plan-level cap on concurrent runs, no penalty for keeping several questions moving at once.

If you've got several questions worth answering, there's no reason to wait for one report to finish before starting the next. Queue them up and let Caspr work through all of them in parallel.

C-07.question: What topics and industries can Caspr analyze?
C-07.answer:
Caspr analyses markets, industries, companies, competitive landscapes, and geographies — any business question you can scope in a prompt. If a serious analyst could research it from credible sources, Caspr can build the report.

In practice, that covers:

- Market sizing — the size, growth, and structure of a market (TAM, SAM, SOM), cited to source.
- Competitive landscapes — the players, their positioning, and share in a given market.
- Company and sector analysis — a named company or a narrow segment, scoped through clarifying questions.
- Industry and geographic deep dives — a sector in a specific country or region.
- Business cases and due-diligence screens — the evidence base behind a decision.

Every analysis draws on 1M+ curated sources — documents, government databases, and news feeds — and cites each insight, so the output holds up under scrutiny wherever the topic sits.

Two honest limits. Very thin or emerging markets have less public data to draw on; where a market is hard to source, a Premium Data Add-on ($20–60, opt-in) pulls in additional premium sources. And Caspr answers business and market questions — it is built for commercial analysis, not legal advice or personal research.

The fastest way to find out whether your question fits is to ask it. Caspr's clarifying questions sharpen the scope before anything runs, so a broad prompt still resolves into a targeted report.

Analyse your market.

C-08.question: Can Caspr analyze a specific company or niche market?
C-08.answer:
Yes. Name the company or the narrow market in your prompt, and Caspr scopes the analysis to it — then sharpens it further through the clarifying questions it asks before running.

For a specific company, say what you need: a competitive profile, a positioning read, a diligence screen, or how it sits within its market. For a niche market, define the boundary — the segment, the geography, the customer — and Caspr builds the report around it rather than defaulting to the broad category.

Every insight is cited to a source drawn from Caspr's 1M+ curated documents, government databases, and news feeds, so a company profile or a niche sizing is one you can put in front of a board and defend.

One honest caveat: the thinner the public record, the less there is to analyse. For a small private company or an emerging niche, expect strong structure and full sourcing on what exists, rather than invented figures to fill gaps — Caspr will not manufacture a number it cannot cite. Where a market is hard to source, a Premium Data Add-on ($20–60, opt-in and priced before the run) pulls in additional premium sources.

For a high-stakes target — an acquisition candidate, an investment, a competitor you are about to move against — run it at Intelligence depth for the broadest sourcing and deepest reasoning.

Analyse a target.

C-09.question: What regions and languages does Caspr cover?
C-09.answer:
Caspr's source base — 1M+ curated documents, government databases and news feeds — spans a broad range of regions, which means most market and industry questions are answerable regardless of where you're asking about. Coverage is not uniform, though: markets with strong public reporting and institutional data produce richer, more heavily cited analyses than markets where credible sourcing is thin on the ground, and that gap reflects the state of available public data, not a limit Caspr imposes deliberately.

Reports themselves are delivered in English. For regions or languages where source coverage is limited, Premium Data Add-ons ($20–60, opt-in, shown before you run) can bring in additional sourcing to close the gap for a specific market.

If your question centres on a region you're unsure about, the fastest way to find out is to ask it — Caspr's clarifying questions will surface if scope needs narrowing before the analysis runs.

[VERIFY: exact list of regions/languages with strong vs. limited source coverage, and whether output languages beyond English are supported, before this goes live.]

Analyse your market.

D-01.question: How to read your Caspr report
D-01.answer:
Every Caspr report opens the same way: an executive summary first, then the analysis, then the sources behind it. Knowing that shape before you start reading turns 100 pages into something you navigate in seconds, not something you scroll through blind.

Start with the **exec summary**. It states the conclusion before the argument — the way a report for a board should. Read it first even if you plan to read everything; it tells you where the sections that follow are going.

From there, the report moves through structured sections — market context, the core analysis, data exhibits — each building on the last. Briefs run flat, one section after another. Studies and Intelligence reports nest: sections carry sub-sections, and the depth of the nesting reflects the depth of the analysis.

You don't have to scroll to find your place. Open **Contents** — the switcher tab beside the report — and you get a table of contents that scroll-syncs with what you're reading: the current section and sub-section highlight as you move, and tapping any row jumps you straight there. It's the fastest way to move through 100 pages without losing your place.

Every insight in the report carries an inline red dot — a citation you can click to see the source behind that specific claim. No hunting for a footnote or a separate sources page; the dot sits right next to the number it's proving. The full source list, if you want everything at once, is the report's final card.

Open the report, read the exec summary, use Contents to move around, click the dots when you want proof. That's the whole system.

Open your report.

D-02.question: What's inside a 100-page report?
D-02.answer:
A Caspr report is built like one a senior analyst would hand to a client, not a pile of generated text. Every section earns its place, and every number in it traces to a source.

It opens with the **executive summary** — the conclusion, stated plainly, before the supporting argument. If a reader has five minutes, this is what they take away.

From there the report moves into **market context** — the landscape your question sits inside: size, structure, the forces shaping it. This is the ground the rest of the analysis stands on.

Next come the **core analysis sections** — the actual work: competitive dynamics, scenario modelling, strategic implications, whatever your prompt and layout called for. This is where the report earns the word "analysis" rather than "summary." Depth scales with tier: a Brief covers this in a few pages; a Study or Intelligence report goes several layers deeper, with nested sub-sections you can navigate from the Contents tab.

Findings are backed by **data exhibits** — charts, tables, and infographics tied directly to the data behind them, not decorative graphics. Each one carries the same citation discipline as the prose around it.

Every insight throughout the report carries an inline red dot you can click to see its source. And at the very end sits the **full source list** — every document, database, and feed the analysis drew on, in one place. No numbered footnotes scattered through the pages, no separate sources tab to dig for.

Conclusion, context, analysis, evidence, sources. The same structure whether the report runs 5 pages or 100.

See a full report.

D-03.question: How do I verify a citation or source?
D-03.answer:
Every insight in a Caspr report carries an inline red dot next to it. That dot is the citation.

Click it, and Caspr answers — through Ask Caspr — with the specific source behind that specific claim. Not a generic reference list, not a footnote number to cross-check against a bibliography: the source for that number, at the point where the number appears.

Do this for any figure in the report, as many times as you want. Trace a market-size estimate to the database it came from. Trace a growth rate to the report it's cited to. If you're about to put a number in front of a board, this is how you confirm it will hold up to the first question asked.

Want everything the report drew on at once, rather than one claim at a time? The full source list sits on the report's **final card** — every document, database, and feed used, in one place.

This is what separates a defensible report from a plausible-sounding one: you can check the work, not just trust it.

Trace an insight.

D-04.question: Can I trust the numbers?
D-04.answer:
Yes — and you don't have to take that on faith, because every number is traceable.

Caspr's numbers come from the **weighing**, a methodology built to reason through data and structure conclusions, not simply generate plausible-sounding text. Behind it sit 1M+ **curated, credible sources** — documents, government databases, news feeds — not scraped web noise. The **sourcing** keeps that data current, so a market-size figure reflects this week's reality, not a training set frozen months ago.

The proof is in the report itself. Every insight carries an inline red dot; click it and Caspr shows the specific source behind that specific claim, right where the claim sits. Nothing in a Caspr report is unsourced — there's nothing left to invent, because every figure is grounded in a citation before it ever reaches the page.

That matters most in the moment you're not thinking about the tool at all — when someone in the room asks where a number came from. You answer with the source, not with "the AI said so."

Zero hallucinations isn't a slogan here. It's what happens when an analysis is built to cite, not to guess.

Verify it yourself.

D-05.question: PDF vs editable PPTX — what's the difference?
D-05.answer:
**PDF** is the finished article — a boardroom-ready report exactly as Caspr produced it, laid out, formatted, ready to send or present as-is. It's included with every analysis, in your language, at no extra cost.

**Editable PPTX** is the same report, restructured into slides you can open in PowerPoint and change — reorder, rewrite, drop into your own template. It unlocks at the **Business milestone**, because editing is a Business-tier feature, not a formatting toggle.

Use the PDF when the report is the deliverable — a standalone document to send to a client or file for the record. Use the PPTX when the report is a starting point — material you need to reshape into your own deck before a meeting.

Both carry every citation. Adapting the PPTX doesn't cost you the sourcing that makes the report defensible in the first place.

Export your report.

D-06.question: What is Intelligence and what makes it deeper?
D-06.answer:
Intelligence is Caspr's deepest analysis depth — built for decisions where being wrong is expensive. Where a Brief answers a single question and a Study builds the full picture, Intelligence goes further on both axes: broader sourcing across the 1M+ document, database, and news-feed library, and more reasoning passes from the assessment stage to stress-test the conclusion before it reaches the page.

The output format doesn't change — still a boardroom-ready PDF or editable PPTX in under 15 minutes, still every insight cited to a credible source. What changes is the rigor behind it: more angles checked, more evidence weighed, a report built to survive scrutiny in a board meeting or an investment committee, not just to inform one.

Pricing reflects the depth. Intelligence runs $300 within a Business or Enterprise Research Budget, or $399 à la carte with no subscription required — useful for a single high-stakes report without committing to a plan. Business is also where Intelligence unlocks in-budget, alongside data upload and editing.

Reach for Intelligence when the decision on the other side of the report matters: due diligence ahead of a term sheet, a market-entry call going to the board, a competitive assessment backing an acquisition. Corporate development teams use it to screen targets; investors, to back a diligence memo the partners will pick apart. For everyday questions, a Study at $80 or a Brief at $15 covers it for less.

Run an Intelligence report.

D-07.question: How do I turn a Caspr report into my board deck?
D-07.answer:
Start with the report you already have, not a blank deck.

At the **Business milestone**, every report includes an **editable PPTX** — the same analysis, restructured into slides rather than pages. Open it in PowerPoint and it behaves like any deck you've built by hand: reorder slides, rewrite headlines, drop in your firm's template and branding.

From there, adapt rather than rebuild. Keep the sections that carry the argument — the exec summary, the core findings, the exhibits that prove them — and cut what your specific audience doesn't need. This is where **Edit mode** earns its keep beforehand too: if a section needs to read differently for this board, revise it in the report first, then export.

The one thing not to do is strip the citations on the way in. Every insight in the PPTX still carries the sourcing it had in the report — keep it. A board deck that can answer "where did this number come from" is a stronger deck than one that can't, and stripping citations to make slides look cleaner throws away Caspr's entire advantage.

Fifteen minutes and an editable deck gets you further than a blank template and a week.

Build your board deck.

E-01.question: How to edit your report
E-01.answer: Editing turns a Caspr report into your report, and it unlocks at the Business milestone. Open any section and Edit mode gives you two ways in: a contextual menu for direct changes — rewrite a paragraph, restructure a section, swap a chart, cut what does not apply — or a rewrite prompt where you describe what you want in plain language and Caspr produces the change for you. Either way, saving creates a new version. Nothing is overwritten; your prior version stays intact on the Versions timeline, so you can always see what changed, compare two readings of the same section, or revert if an edit did not land the way you wanted. Editing is where a Caspr report stops being a one-shot deliverable and starts being a working document you shape. Sharpen the language for a specific audience, restructure the flow to match how your board reads a deck, cut a section that does not apply to this meeting, or push a chart to say what the underlying data actually supports more clearly than the default view did. Citations move with the content, so a rewritten paragraph is still traceable to its original source — editing never breaks the trail back to where a number came from. Editing is the step between a boardroom-ready report and a report that is boardroom-ready for your board specifically, in your language, in your structure, in the order you would present it. If your account has not reached Business, this single capability is the clearest reason to upgrade — everything else about the report is already yours to keep. A consultant tailoring the same market research for three different clients, or an investor trimming a due-diligence report down to what the IC actually needs to see, both live in Edit mode more than anywhere else in the product.

E-02.question: How to export to PowerPoint
E-02.answer: Exporting to PowerPoint gives you an editable PPTX — the deck version of your report, built to be dropped into your own template rather than presented exactly as Caspr delivered it. Editable PPTX unlocks at the Business milestone, alongside the rest of Caspr's editing tools, since adapting a deck properly usually means editing it first. From the report, open Outputs, choose PPTX, and pick the language you need it in; it renders natively in that language rather than translating after the fact, and it is priced per output if it falls outside your tier's included base formats. Once exported, the deck holds the same structure, charts, and citations as the PDF version — just reflowed into slide form, ready to be re-themed in your own colours, trimmed to the slides you actually need, or dropped straight into a client or board template. This is the fastest route from a Caspr report to a deck you walk into a meeting with: export the PPTX, adapt it using Edit mode and your own template, and keep the numbers and the sourcing intact underneath every slide.

E-03.question: How to request a follow-up analysis
E-03.answer: A follow-up analysis lets you keep working with a report instead of starting over each time a new question occurs to you — Caspr as an ongoing dialogue with your material, not a single answer delivered once and done. It unlocks at the Business milestone, alongside section refinement, since both draw on the same editing engine. From any section, open Edit mode and use the rewrite prompt to ask Caspr to go deeper: expand a section, address a question the original brief never scoped, or build out an angle the report only touched on in passing. Caspr treats that as a targeted extension of the existing analysis, grounded in the same underlying sources rather than started fresh, and saving the result produces a new version on your report's Versions timeline, sitting alongside every prior read of the report. This is the analyst dialogue a one-shot tool cannot offer: you read the report, a real question occurs to you on page forty, and you put it back to Caspr directly without re-running the whole analysis or losing the work already done getting here. Follow-ups draw from your Research Budget like any generation, scoped and priced to what you are actually asking for rather than the full report — going deeper on one question costs a fraction of starting over. Use it the way you would use a second meeting with the analyst who wrote the first draft, not a request to start again. You read a market sizing Study, and the number that jumps out is the competitive intensity in one sub-segment — instead of commissioning a whole new Competitive Landscape brief, you ask Caspr to build that section out inside the report you already have, and it arrives as an addition to the analysis you were already holding, not a disconnected second document to reconcile against the first.

E-04.question: How to refine one section without re-running everything
E-04.answer: You do not need to re-run an entire report to fix or deepen one part of it. Open the section that needs work in Edit mode, use the contextual menu or the rewrite prompt to describe exactly what should change, and save — only that section is touched, nothing else moves. The rest of the report, and every citation in it, stays exactly as it was before you opened the editor. This is deliberately narrower than requesting a full follow-up analysis: you are not extending the report's scope, just sharpening what is already there — tightening a paragraph that ran long, correcting emphasis that landed wrong, asking for a table instead of a block of prose, or swapping a chart for one that makes the point faster. Because the change is scoped to a single section rather than the whole document, it costs less than a full re-analysis and returns faster too. Saving still produces a new version on your Versions timeline, so the prior read of that section is never lost — you can always compare or revert. Section refinement unlocks at the Business milestone, the same gate as editing generally. It is the tool for the common case: the report is right almost everywhere, and exactly one section needs another pass before it goes out the door.

F-01.question: How does Caspr pricing work?
F-01.answer:
Caspr runs on a Research Budget — one monthly number that funds every analysis you run. No stacked subscription tiers, no token metering, no line-item invoice to decode.

You set a Research Budget, and each analysis draws from it at a fixed price: Brief $15, Study $80, Intelligence $300 in-budget ($399 à la carte), plus an optional Premium Data Add-on ($20–$60) shown and confirmed before the analysis starts. Whatever you don't spend carries forward automatically — you're billed for what you use, not for a plan you didn't touch.

The size of your Research Budget determines what you can access:

- Professional — $200/month, roughly $186 available for analyses. Brief and Study.
- Business — $600/month, roughly $558 available. Adds Intelligence, data upload, output editing, and follow-up refinement.
- Enterprise — $1,800/month, roughly $1,674 available, pooled across a team of three seats. Adds SSO and API access.

You're charged once a month. No separate bills for individual reports, no per-seat add-ons layered on top.

Before committing to a monthly number, start with the $100 Research Budget every new account receives free — no card required — and see exactly what $15 and $80 buy. See plans.

F-02.question: What is a Research Budget?
F-02.answer:
A Research Budget is the single number you authorise each month — a pool of spend you draw analyses from, not a licence per seat or a fixed subscription tier.

Think of it as a research retainer you control directly, the way you'd control a budget line for external research, except you decide exactly how it gets spent, analysis by analysis. Every Brief, Study, or Intelligence analysis carries a fixed price, shown before you commit. Running one simply draws from the balance — no separate access fee to track, no token metering, no seat-by-seat billing to reconcile.

Unused balance carries forward automatically. Set a $200 budget and spend only $80 in a month, and the remaining balance isn't lost — it sits in your Wallet, ready for next month's analyses, on top of whatever the next recharge adds.

The budget amount also determines which features unlock — Business and Enterprise sit at higher thresholds — but that's a separate question from how much of it you spend in a given month.

New accounts start with a $100 gifted Research Budget, no credit card required, so you can run real analyses before committing to anything.

Start with $100 free.

F-03.question: How much does each analysis cost?
F-03.answer:
Four prices, no fine print.

- Brief — $15. A focused 3–5 page briefing, ready in about 15 minutes.
- Study — $80. The full analysis: methodology, scenario work, a boardroom-ready PDF or editable PPTX.
- Intelligence — $300 drawn from your Research Budget, or $399 as a one-off with no subscription required. The deepest depth, built for board-level and diligence-grade decisions.
- Premium Data Add-on — $20–$60, only when an analysis calls for a source like Bloomberg or specialist regulatory data. You see the exact price and approve it before it's added.

The $200,000 question a strategy engagement would spend weeks answering costs $80 here, delivered in minutes, not months.

Every price is fixed and shown upfront — no metered tokens, no per-page charges, no surprise invoice after the report lands. Run one from $15.

F-04.question: What happens to unused budget?
F-04.answer:
Nothing happens to it — unused Research Budget carries forward automatically. You don't lose what you didn't spend.

Each month, Caspr recharges only the amount you actually used the month before — a delta recharge, not a flat renewal. Say you set a $200 budget: run one Study ($80) in a given month, and your next recharge restores only that $80. The rest of your balance, untouched, carries straight through to the new cycle rather than resetting to zero and forcing you to start over.

This is the default behaviour, not a setting to configure or a perk to request. There's no "use it or lose it" clock on your working balance, and no monthly allowance that expires unused. Your balance simply reflects real usage, cycle over cycle, for as long as the account stays active.

The only balances that do expire are gifted ones — your free trial's Research Budget, which has a 90-day window, and any promotional credits, which carry their own shorter terms. Balance you've paid for stays yours until you spend it.

See how budget works.

F-05.question: What's included at each plan?
F-05.answer:
Three milestones — Professional, Business, and Enterprise — determine what's unlocked as your Research Budget grows. All three run the same core loop: prompt, layout, gate, boardroom-ready report. What changes across them is analysis depth, editing power, and team scale.

**Professional — $200/month budget, roughly $186 available for analyses.** The entry point for solo use. Run Brief and Study depth analyses — from a 3–5 page briefing note to a full weighing engagement with scenario analysis. You also get a standing Monthly Brief on a topic of your choosing and one Caspr Signals topic for weekly developments.
