[VERIFY: confirm target response time / support hours before publishing.]

Contact support.

J-01.question: What is Analytical AI?
J-01.answer: Analytical AI is artificial intelligence purpose-built to analyze data, structure conclusions, and cite every source — not to hold a conversation. Where generative AI predicts plausible-sounding text, Analytical AI reasons through evidence and delivers a decision-ready report. It is the model behind Caspr: put in a question, get back a cited, boardroom-ready analysis. Learn more.

J-02.question: How does Caspr handle sources that disagree?
J-02.answer: Assessment is Caspr's research methodology: it reasons through data and structures conclusions, rather than retrieving and repeating snippets. It decides what a report needs, in what order, and how each finding supports the next — the way a research desk plans an analysis before writing it. Every Caspr report runs on it. Learn more.

J-03.question: How current is Caspr's data?
J-03.answer: Sourcing is Caspr's real-time live data layer — continuous feeds from documents, government databases, and news sources that keep every analysis current. Rather than reasoning from a training cutoff, Caspr pulls today's data into today's report, so a market that moved this quarter shows up in the numbers, not last year's snapshot. Learn more.

J-04.question: What is a Research Budget?
J-04.answer: A Research Budget is the monthly pool of spend a Caspr plan grants — Professional, Business, or Enterprise — from which each analysis is drawn at a fixed price: $15 for a Brief, $80 for a Study, $300 for Intelligence. One charge a month, no surprise line items. Unused balance carries forward automatically, so nothing you don't spend is lost. Learn more.

J-05.question: What are Brief, Study and Intelligence?
J-05.answer: Brief, Study, and Intelligence are Caspr's three analysis depths, not different products — the difference is how far the analysis goes. Brief ($15) answers a specific question fast. Study ($80) builds the full picture. Intelligence ($300 in-budget, $399 à la carte) is the deepest: board-grade, for decisions with real stakes. All three arrive as a cited, boardroom-ready report. Learn more.

J-06.question: What is a boardroom-ready report?
J-06.answer: A boardroom-ready report is Caspr's standard output: a roughly 100-page, presentation-quality PDF or editable PPTX, structured and designed to be put in front of decision-makers without rework. Every insight is cited to its source, so the numbers can be defended on the spot, not just presented. It is the deliverable, not a draft. Learn more.

J-07.question: What is a citation in a Caspr report?
J-07.answer: A citation is the credible source shown next to every insight in a Caspr report — a document, government database, or news feed the claim can be traced back to. Nothing is asserted without one, which is how a Caspr report stays verifiable instead of asking to be taken on faith. Learn more.

J-08.question: What is the layout proposal?
J-08.answer: The layout proposal is the structured skeleton Caspr proposes right after your prompt — the report's sections and flow, before any research runs. You confirm it or adjust it, and a few clarifying questions sharpen it further, so the analysis that follows is built to the shape you actually need. Learn more.

A-12.question: What happens when I sign up?
A-12.answer:
Signup drops you straight into the tool — there is no setup wizard, no onboarding tour to click through, no profile to fill in first. You land directly in the prompt box, ready to run your first analysis.

Type a single-line prompt, and Caspr proposes a structured layout — the report's skeleton — and asks a few clarifying questions to scope it to your actual question rather than a generic version of it. From there, the first real checkpoint is the **gate**: one screen showing exactly what's about to be produced — Type and Tier, output formats, language, style, and price — before anything runs. Everything on it is pre-set by Caspr, and everything is changeable if you want a different depth or format.

Your **$100 Research Budget** arrives with your account and covers your first run outright, with room to spare. There's no credit card at signup, no plan to pick, no trial clock beyond the 90-day expiry on the budget itself — just an email address and a prompt.

From the gate, hitting Generate commits the run. Generation is atomic once it starts, so most analyses finish in under 15 minutes, and you can watch the build in Theater or step away entirely and come back to a finished report.

That's the whole path from signup to your first boardroom-ready report: prompt, layout, questions, gate, done.

Start your first analysis.

C-10.question: What is the gate before I generate?
C-10.answer:
The gate is the single confirmation before Caspr generates anything. Nothing runs until you've seen it and hit Generate — there's no second checkpoint after this one, and no surprise step buried later in the process.

It shows you everything about to happen in one place: the Type and Tier — Brief, Study, or Intelligence — the output formats, the language, the style, any Premium Data Add-on you've opted into, and the price. Caspr pre-sets every one of these based on your prompt and layout, so you're reviewing a proposal Caspr already built for you, not filling out a form from scratch. And every one of them is changeable, right there on the same screen, before you commit.

The red Generate button carries the running total. As you adjust anything on the gate — swap a format, add a language, opt into an add-on — the number on that button updates in real time, so what you're about to spend is never a surprise buried in a follow-up invoice. Hit Generate, and the analysis begins: atomic, no pausing, no mid-run edits, delivered in minutes.

The gate exists so the only thing you ever confirm blind is the prompt itself, back at the very start. Everything downstream of it — scope, format, price — you approve first, in full view, before Caspr spends a cent of your budget.

It's a single screen, not a checkout flow with pages to click through. Everything you'd need to sign off on a report sits together: what it is, what it costs, what you'll get back. That's deliberate — the layout already did the work of confirming scope, so the gate isn't asking you to re-decide what the report is about. It's asking you to confirm how it gets delivered, and for how much, one last time before Caspr commits the budget and starts the clock.

C-11.question: Can I change the report before it generates?
C-11.answer:
Yes. At the gate, before you hit Generate, you can change the Tier, output formats, language, and style — all of it, from the same screen.

Formats, language, and style are the easy changes: adjust any of them and the price on the Generate button updates immediately, no rebuild, no re-review needed. Change your mind on PPTX versus PDF, add a second language, or switch the style, and you're straight back to confirming — nothing else about the report resets.

Tier is the one that costs you something to change. Brief, Study, and Intelligence aren't the same report at different lengths — they're structurally different, with different sections and different depth — so switching Tier rebuilds the layout from scratch and brings you back through the layout screen before you reach the gate again. Caspr warns you once before this happens, because the layout you already approved won't come back once you confirm the switch; you'll be reviewing a new one built for the new Tier.

So adjust freely on formats, language, and style at the gate. Think before you touch Tier — you're choosing a different report, not resizing the one you already reviewed.

Why the warning matters: the layout you approved reflected real thought — sections you added, ones you cut, an order you set deliberately. Rebuilding for a new Tier discards that work and starts over, because a Brief's flat structure and an Intelligence report's nested one aren't the same skeleton at different sizes. Caspr flags it once, clearly, so the decision to trade your approved layout for a different Tier is one you make on purpose, not one you back into by accident.

C-12.question: Can I pause or stop a report while it generates?
C-12.answer:
No. Once you pass the gate, generation is atomic — there's no pause button, no stop, and no editing mid-run. Caspr commits to the report it's building and finishes it start to finish.

That's deliberate. A report assembled from interrupted, half-changed instructions isn't one you'd trust putting in front of a board, so Caspr doesn't build one that way. It runs the analysis straight through, the same way an analyst wouldn't hand you a memo rewritten mid-sentence by a change of brief.

While it works, you're not stuck watching a progress bar with nothing to do. Open Theater to watch the report build in real time, section by section, or pull out Ask Caspr in the side drawer to ask questions or answer Caspr's get-to-know prompts while you wait. Neither one changes the report underway — they're there for you, not for the run, and collapsing the drawer just returns you to the full Theater view.

Once the report is finished, that's when change happens — through Edit mode, where every revision produces a new version you can compare against the last. Nothing you want to adjust is lost by waiting. It's just that the report has to exist before there's something to edit.

D-08.question: What output formats do I get?
D-08.answer:
It depends on the analysis depth.

A **Brief** delivers **PDF** and **Markdown**. A **Study** or **Intelligence** report delivers **PDF, PPTX, XLSX, CSV, and Markdown** — the full set, not a subset you have to unlock.

That base set is included in the analysis price, generated natively in your own language — not English, translated after the fact. You choose formats and language at the **gate**, before the report runs.

Want something beyond the base — an extra format, a second language? Each one is generated and priced as its own output: PDF, DOCX, XLSX, and CSV run **$5**; PPTX runs **$10**; Markdown is always free. Add them at the gate or later from the **Outputs** tab — either way, the price sums into the button before you commit. [VERIFY exact figures vs .agents/pricing-model.md §4.6]

Generate your report.

D-09.question: Can I get my report in another language?
D-09.answer:
Yes. English isn't assumed and it isn't a default you're stuck with — Caspr is multilingual by default, and your working language is included in the base price, generated natively in that language rather than translated after the fact.

Each **additional** language is its own output — a full rewrite of the report, not a format swap — generated in whatever formats you choose and priced per output, the same table used for extra formats. [VERIFY per-language pricing vs .agents/pricing-model.md §4.6]

Pick your languages at the **gate**, before the report runs, or add more later from the **Outputs** tab without touching the underlying analysis. Either way, the report you already have stays exactly as it is — you're only choosing what gets rendered from it, and in which language.

Add a language.

D-10.question: Can I change the report's style or template?
D-10.answer:
At launch, Caspr runs on a single template — one style, applied consistently across every report.

Style is doing more work than it sounds like. It governs density, vocabulary, how charts are treated, overall length, and whether appendices appear — the texture of the report, not just its skin. You set it before generating, at the **gate**, and choosing it there costs nothing.

Changing style **after** generation is a different action. "Make it denser," "add an appendix," "more visual" — each of these is a re-generation, not a preference toggle, and it's metered as an output like any other post-generation change.

Custom, user-built templates aren't part of the launch scope — one Caspr-designed template, well executed, beats a menu of half-finished ones.

Set your style.

D-11.question: What is Ask Caspr?
D-11.answer: Ask Caspr is the conversation that lives with your report — a scoped analyst you can question about the work in front of you, not a general chatbot. Open the Ask tab and you will find two things: a read-only history of everything Caspr already asked and confirmed while scoping your brief, sitting above a live question box. Type a question about a number, a claim, or a section you want explained differently, and Caspr answers from your report and its underlying sources — nothing outside that scope, nothing speculative, and nothing pulled from a different analysis you have run. Ask why a competitor was ranked ahead of another, where a growth figure came from, or what the layout deliberately left out, and you get an answer grounded in the same sources the report itself was built on. Ask Caspr is live from the moment generation starts, not just after delivery. Watching the Theater build your report and want to know why a section is structured a certain way, ask. Waiting through a 15-minute run and want to sharpen your Research profile for future analyses, Caspr's get-to-know questions surface here too. One rule matters more than the rest: asking never changes the report. The Ask tab is for reading and questioning, not writing. If a question surfaces something you actually want changed — a section rewritten, a chart swapped, a claim restated — that happens in Edit mode, and it produces a new version. Ask Caspr is where you interrogate the analysis. Edit is where you act on it. Treat it as a standing line to the analyst who wrote the report, open for as long as the report exists — no extra charge, no time limit.

D-12.question: How do citations work in my report?
D-12.answer: Every insight in your report carries an inline red dot. Click it, and Caspr answers with the source behind that specific claim — scoped through Ask Caspr, without leaving the page. No footnote to hunt for, no separate Sources tab to open, no page number to cross-reference. The number stays on screen; the source arrives right next to it, in context, the moment you ask. This is what makes a Caspr report defensible in a room where someone will ask where a figure came from. You are not trusting the claim on faith — you are tracing it, one click at a time, to a named, credible source, and you can keep asking follow-up questions about that same source if you need more than the citation alone gives you. The full reference list for the entire report lives on its own card at the very end — a complete bibliography, in case you want to review every source at once rather than one insight at a time, or hand it to someone doing their own diligence. Day to day, though, you will rarely need it: the red dot does the work of a footnote without the friction of one. This mechanic runs on the same engine as the rest of Ask Caspr — the same scoped, report-specific answers, just triggered by a click instead of typed by you. It applies to every insight in every section, from the executive summary through the data exhibits and appendices. If a number appears in your report, it carries a red dot, and that red dot has an answer waiting behind it. That is the standard analyst-grade output has to clear: not just a confident claim, but a claim you can defend, live, to whoever in the room asks first.

D-13.question: What are Versions?
D-13.answer: Versions is your report's timeline. Every edit you save creates a new version, and the Versions tab shows them in order — v1, v2, v3 — as rows you can open individually to read that state of the report in full. Beneath each version sit its outputs: the actual generated files, PDF, PPTX, and the rest, produced from that specific version. Outputs are pinned to the version they came from. Generate a PDF off v2, then edit again to reach v3, and that PDF still belongs to v2 — it does not silently update to reflect your latest changes. If you want a current file, you generate a new output from whichever version you are now on. This matters because it means nothing is ever quietly overwritten. An earlier version and the outputs generated from it stay exactly as they were, so you can compare what changed between two versions, revert to an earlier read of the analysis if a later edit went the wrong way, or hand a colleague the exact file you reviewed together last week without worrying it has since moved. Outputs are generated on command, not automatically on every edit — so editing a report does not quietly spend budget regenerating every file behind it in the background. You choose when a version is worth turning into a deliverable, and which format that deliverable should take. It also gives you an honest audit trail: if a stakeholder asks what changed between the draft you shared on Monday and the one you presented on Friday, the timeline answers that question without you having to remember.

D-14.question: What is the Contents view?
D-14.answer: Contents is your report's table of contents, and it moves with you as you read. As you scroll through the report, the current section and sub-section highlight in Contents automatically — you always know exactly where you are inside a hundred pages, even without looking at a page number. Tap any row and the report jumps straight to it, no scrolling required to get there. It works the other way too: keep reading normally and Contents keeps updating to track you. That two-way sync is what makes a long report navigable rather than a wall of text you have to scroll through blind, section by section, to find the one page you actually need. A Brief's Contents is flat — a short, single-level list, matching its tighter three-to-five-page scope. Study and Intelligence reports nest: sections expand into sub-sections in the list itself, mirroring the deeper structure those tiers deliver across a hundred pages. Use Contents to orient yourself the moment a report lands, to jump straight to the section a colleague asked about before a call, or simply to check how much ground the analysis actually covers before you commit to reading it end to end. It functions the way a bookmark pane does in a well-built PDF, except it already knows where you are without you telling it — useful when you are moving between the executive summary and a data exhibit thirty pages apart while prepping talking points for a meeting.

D-15.question: What are Updates?
D-15.answer: Updates is coming soon — not yet available. Once live, it will flag when new data could change a finding in a report you have already run, so a standing analysis can be refreshed with what has changed rather than rebuilt from scratch. Watch this space; for now, re-run a fresh analysis if the market has moved since your last report.

D-16.question: What is Theater?
D-16.answer: Theater is the immersive view you get while Caspr works — a live look at your analysis being built, section by section, rather than a spinner and a wait with nothing to show for it. Stay on it and you watch the report take shape in real time, the same structure you confirmed at the gate filling in with research as it happens. Open the side drawer and Ask Caspr sits alongside it: ask a question about what is being researched right now, or answer the short get-to-know prompts Caspr uses to sharpen your Research profile for future reports, all without losing sight of the build behind it. Collapse the drawer and you are back to the full Theater view, no progress lost either way. Nothing you do here — watching, asking, answering — touches the report itself. Generation is atomic once it starts: no pause, no stop, no mid-run edit, by design. Theater is where you spend the wait, not where you steer the outcome. If something needs to change once you see it, that happens after delivery, in Edit mode. Most reports finish inside 15 minutes, so Theater is built for a wait that short — something to watch, not a dashboard you need to babysit for an hour. It is also where the sourcing stage's live sourcing becomes visible: instead of a blank progress bar, you see the categories of research the analysis is actually pulling from as it works.

D-17.question: What are the charts and visuals in my report?
D-17.answer: Caspr renders its findings as charts, tables, and infographics inside the report — a number rarely stands alone when a visual makes the finding clearer to a reader skimming for the headline. Every one of them is tied to its cited data, so a chart is not decoration sitting next to a claim; it is the claim, rendered, with the same sourcing standard as the surrounding text. Want something different once you see it? Open Edit mode on any visual and you can swap a chart type, adjust a table, or ask Caspr for a different treatment entirely — a bar chart instead of a line, a ranked table instead of a paragraph, a simplified view for a slide instead of a dense one for a page. Saving that change produces a new version, alongside any text edits you have made elsewhere in the report, and the prior version of the visual stays on the Versions timeline if you want it back. Charts and standard infographics render deterministically, so revising them is fast and does not touch the underlying data. A limited number of bespoke visual generations are included with each analysis, scaled to its tier, which covers the shaping most reports actually need before you run out. Every visual carries the same red-dot citation as the text around it, so a chart is exactly as traceable as the sentence describing it — nothing in the report gets to make a claim the rest of it does not have to answer for.

E-05.question: How do I get more formats or languages after generating?
E-05.answer: Generating additional formats or languages after delivery happens from the Outputs tab. Open Generate Output and you will see the same selector you saw at the gate before your first run — pick any format or language you have not already received, and each one is priced per output as you add it to the queue. Choices queue as individual cards, format and language and price shown together on each, and every card you add sums into the Generate button so you always see the running total before you commit to anything. Remove a card before generating if you change your mind about a format. The Tier and the underlying data behind your report stay fixed here — you are not re-running the analysis, re-scoping the layout, or changing what was researched, only choosing what to render from work Caspr has already completed. That keeps this fast: no clarifying questions to answer again, no layout to reconfirm, just format, language, and a clear price before you generate. Use it when a colleague needs the deck in French, when a base PDF was enough at first but you now want the XLSX behind the numbers, or when a stakeholder in another market needs the whole report translated into their language. Everything generated here is pinned to the version you generated it from, and shows up as a card on that version's row in Versions, exactly like any other output. Formats you already received as part of your base tier are marked as such, so you are never charged twice for a file you already have sitting in your report.

G-08.question: Where do I see my balance and spending?
G-08.answer:
Open your **Wallet** — it's the single screen for everything about what you have and what you've spent.

At the top: your spendable Research Budget balance, the amount actually available to run analyses right now. Below it, an **activity ledger** — every analysis you've run, what it cost, and when, itemised individually rather than lumped into one monthly total. Run a Study and a Brief in the same week, and the ledger shows both, separately, at their fixed prices.

Your **next recharge** date and amount are shown too. Caspr recharges only what you spent the cycle before, so this number moves with your actual usage rather than sitting at a fixed monthly figure.

Invoices are downloadable directly from the ledger, one per billing cycle, ready for expensing or bookkeeping without digging through email.

One terminology note worth internalising: this is a **budget**, not a plan. There's no seat count to manage, no feature tier to remember — just a number you control and a balance that reflects exactly what you've used.

If your balance runs low, Wallet is also where you top it up or raise your monthly budget.

Open your Wallet.

G-09.question: How does Caspr learn about me (Research profile)?
G-09.answer:
Caspr occasionally asks a short question inside the Ask Caspr thread — your role, the industries you follow, the kind of decisions your analyses tend to support. Nothing that blocks the report you're waiting on; answer it or skip it and keep going.

Each answer sharpens your **Research profile** — a running record of what Caspr knows about you, used to fit future analyses to your actual work rather than starting from a generic template every time. Ask the same market-sizing question as a PE analyst and as a category manager, and the two reports come back differently scoped, in part because of what's in each profile.

Every fact Caspr has learned is listed in your Research profile screen, in plain language — nothing inferred silently and hidden from view. If something's wrong, outdated, or you'd simply rather Caspr forget it, remove it with one tap. There's no bulk reset required to correct a single fact.

Two things worth being clear on: answering these questions is entirely optional, and it never changes or blocks the report currently generating. The profile shapes future analyses, not the one already in progress.

Want a full clean slate instead of removing facts one at a time? That's what Reset is for — it clears the whole profile at once, while keeping your account and wallet balance intact.

Sharpen your profile.

G-10.question: How do I change my language or output style?
G-10.answer:
Open **Preferences** from your account. It holds three defaults Caspr applies to every new analysis: your language, your output style, and your preferred format.

Set your language once — French, say — and every new report generates natively in French from the start, written that way, not English translated afterward. Output style governs how the report actually reads: vocabulary, chart treatment, appendices, overall length and density. Format sets which file type Caspr produces by default when a new analysis completes.

None of this locks you in per analysis. At the **gate**, before any specific report generates, you can override any of these defaults for that one run — send one analysis out in Spanish while your account default stays English, without touching Preferences at all.

Changing your defaults in Preferences doesn't reach back into reports already generated; it only applies going forward, from the next analysis you run.

Open Preferences.

G-11.question: How do I secure my account?
G-11.answer:
Everything account security lives on one screen: **Security**, under your account settings.

**Password** — change it any time; you'll need your current password to confirm the change, standard practice against anyone who's gained partial access.

**Two-factor authentication** — enable it to add a second check on sign-in, beyond just your password. An authenticator app is the recommended method over SMS, which is more vulnerable to interception and SIM-swap attacks.

**Devices** — a list of everything currently signed in to your account. If you don't recognise one, or you've simply lost a laptop, sign it out from here directly, without needing to change your password first.

[VERIFY: exact two-factor methods offered (authenticator app, SMS, or both) and the specific device-list controls (per-device sign-out vs. a single "sign out everywhere") with the engineering team before publishing.]

None of this is optional friction — it's the same discipline you'd expect from any tool holding boardroom-sensitive analysis. Caspr is ISO 27001:2022 certified and GDPR compliant; account-level security is the layer you control directly, on top of that.

Open Security.

G-12.question: What's the difference between resetting and deleting my account?
G-12.answer:
**Reset** is the clean slate. It forgets your Research profile and deletes your existing reports, but your account stays open and your **wallet balance is untouched** — you keep what you've paid for and can start running fresh analyses immediately afterward. Reset is what you want when you're changing how you use Caspr, not whether you use it at all — a new client, a new research focus, a profile that's drifted from what you actually need.

**Delete** closes the account entirely. It's final: your remaining Research Budget balance is **forfeited**, not refunded, and there's no walking it back once it's done. To confirm, you type the word DELETE — deliberately, so it can't happen from a stray click.

Both actions ask for explicit confirmation before doing anything irreversible; neither fires from a single misclick or an accidental tap. If you're not sure which you want, Reset is the safer default — it clears the slate without giving up the balance you've already funded.

Manage your account.

G-13.question: How do I get help or contact support?
G-13.answer:
Open **Get Help** from the navigation — it's built as a searchable FAQ first, a message form second, because most answers don't need a person to deliver them.

Search directly for what you're stuck on, or browse by category: **Basics, Analyses, Pricing, Reports, Account**. Expand any answer inline, right where you found it — no separate page to load, no ticket to open for something the FAQ already covers.

If the FAQ genuinely doesn't answer it, use **Message support**. It pre-tags your message with whatever category you were browsing when you opened it, so support already has context before you've finished typing a word. Add a subject line, describe the issue, and send — no need to re-explain where in the product you ran into it.

[VERIFY: support response-time commitment before stating an SLA publicly.]

Get Help is designed so you don't need the exact right words for your problem. Search loosely, browse by category, or skip straight to messaging a person if you'd rather not hunt for the answer yourself. Most account and pricing questions are already answered inline — Message support exists for what's genuinely specific to you.

Open Get Help.

K-01.question: What is the Data Room?
K-01.answer:
The Data Room is where your uploaded files live, and where you decide what Caspr is allowed to use. Every file you bring in sits in one of three groups.

**Included** files are attached to your analyses by default — Caspr draws on them automatically alongside its own 1M+ curated sources, no extra step required each time you run an analysis.

**Excluded** files stay in your Data Room but sit out of every analysis unless you opt them in for a specific run. Nothing is deleted; it's simply not in default use, which keeps a one-off document from quietly bleeding into unrelated reports.

**Connected** sources — your own subscriptions to Bloomberg, Refinitiv, S&P Capital IQ, or PitchBook, feeding straight into your analyses — are coming soon. Not yet live, so don't expect them in the Data Room today.

Uploading your own data unlocks at the Business milestone. Once unlocked, it's how you fold proprietary numbers, internal decks, or a client's own data room into a Caspr analysis, rather than working from public sources alone — useful for due diligence, a client-specific business case, or any report that needs to reflect information Caspr can't find on its own.

Everything in the Data Room defaults to Private, stays under your control, and can be moved between Included and Excluded, or deleted outright, at any time.

This is the mechanic behind due diligence: upload the data room, mark the files Included, and Caspr wraps the market intelligence around them — the investment memo builds itself from your numbers plus Caspr's own sources, rather than from your numbers alone.

K-02.question: What file types can I upload?
K-02.answer:
Caspr accepts four file types: PDF, XLSX, CSV, and DOCX. Upload several at once — there's no one-at-a-time limit, so a full data room's worth of files can go in together.

No file in hand? Paste a link instead — an article, a dataset, a public report — and Caspr fetches and indexes it the same way it would a document you'd uploaded directly, no separate step required.

Whatever you add, whether uploaded or linked, is folded into your analyses alongside Caspr's 1M+ curated sources, so your own numbers sit next to the market data Caspr already draws on, rather than existing as a separate, disconnected layer.

Data upload is a feature of the Business milestone — see what unlocks at Business if your account isn't there yet. Below that, you're working from Caspr's own sources alone.

A pasted link works best for something public and citable — a press release, a regulatory filing, a published dataset. For anything internal or confidential, upload the file directly rather than linking to it, so it stays private to your account from the start rather than depending on a link staying live.

K-03.question: How do I upload a file?
K-03.answer:
Open the Data Room and use the add-file panel. On desktop, drop your files onto the upload box or click it to browse; on mobile, tap Upload files. No file in hand — paste a link underneath instead, and Caspr fetches and indexes it directly, without needing a downloaded copy first.

New files land at the top of your Included list immediately, each with its own progress bar while it processes. You don't have to wait for one to finish before adding the next — keep dropping files in and they'll queue and complete independently, so a large batch doesn't force you to sit and watch.

Every upload defaults to Private, kept to your account and visible only to you. If a file should be shared more broadly, change that from the file's menu once it lands — Private is the safe default, so there's nothing extra to set on the way in, only a deliberate choice to make afterward if you want otherwise.

Once a file has finished processing, it's ready to use — Caspr will draw on it automatically the next time you run an analysis, since new uploads land in Included by default. Move it to Excluded from the same menu if you'd rather keep it on hand without it feeding every future report.

K-04.question: What's the difference between Private and Public files?
K-04.answer:
Every file in your Data Room carries a Private or Public tag, visible at a glance from its menu. Private is the default for every upload — the file stays to your account, and only you can see or use it in an analysis.

Making a file Public is always a deliberate choice, made explicitly from the file's menu — it never happens by default, and it's never a side effect of uploading or of running an analysis. Reversing it is just as easy: switching a file back to Private is always allowed instantly, with no confirmation step, because leaving something Public by mistake is the costly error, and Caspr is built to make that one easy to undo, not the one that's easy to make.

[VERIFY exact Public-file semantics — what "Public" makes visible, to whom, and under what conditions — with the team before publishing.]

Check or change a file's visibility any time from its menu in the Data Room; there's no separate settings screen to hunt through.

Keep board-sensitive material — an internal deck, a client's data room, anything you wouldn't forward without thinking — set to Private by default and leave it there unless you have a specific reason to change it.

K-05.question: What do Included and Excluded mean?
K-05.answer:
Included and Excluded are the two states a file can sit in while it stays in your Data Room — the difference is whether Caspr uses it automatically, not whether it's kept.

**Included** files are attached to your analyses by default. Upload something and it starts here, folded into every run alongside Caspr's own sources, unless you deliberately move it out.

**Excluded** files are kept, not deleted, but sit out of analyses unless you opt them into a specific run. Use this for a file you want on hand without it bleeding into every report — a one-off document, something outdated, or data relevant to only a single project.

Move a file between the two from its menu. Moving to Excluded is instant, since you're only narrowing what gets used and nothing downstream depends on it. Moving back to Included takes a one-tap confirm, since it reopens the file to default use across every future analysis — a small, deliberate step for a change with much wider reach.

A typical case: last quarter's internal deck was useful when it was current, but you don't want it quietly informing every new analysis six months on. Move it to Excluded instead of deleting it — it stays available to opt into a specific run later, without shaping reports it no longer belongs in.

K-06.question: How do I stop Caspr using a file without deleting it?
K-06.answer:
Open the file's menu in your Data Room and select Move to Excluded. It's instant, no confirmation needed, and the file stays exactly where it is, just out of the default set Caspr draws on. Excluded files are never attached to an analysis automatically; they only get pulled in if you opt them into that specific run.

This is the move to reach for whenever you're not sure you'll need the file long-term, rather than deleting it: nothing is lost, and nothing about the file changes except that Caspr stops assuming it's relevant. If you want it back in default rotation later, move it back to Included from the same menu — that direction takes a one-tap confirm, since it re-opens the file to every analysis again.

Deleting is the one step you can't undo. Excluding is the one you can flip either direction, as often as you like.

K-07.question: How do I delete a file?
K-07.answer:
Open the file's menu in your Data Room and select Delete. A confirmation appears before anything happens — deletion is the one action here you can't reverse, so Caspr makes you pass through it deliberately.

That confirmation offers you an out: Move to Excluded instead. Excluding takes the file out of default use without destroying it — it stays in your Data Room, available to opt into a specific analysis later. If you're deleting because you don't want the file used automatically, that's usually the answer you actually want, and it costs you nothing to keep.

Choose Delete permanently only when you mean the copy gone for good. Once confirmed, Caspr cannot re-attach the file to any future analysis — not the current one, not one you run next year. There's no recovery and no second confirmation after the first.

Deleting has no effect on analyses that already used the file — the report you generated keeps its citations. Only future runs lose access to the source.

When in doubt, exclude first. Delete when you're certain.
